To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a bipolar lightning flash containing two first positive strokes followed by multiple negative strokes is possible.

we measured electric and magnetic fields of a cloud-to ground lightning flash containing two first strokes, one positive and one negative, separated in time and in ground strike locations, followed by four subsequent negative strokes.

we observed a lightning flash with two initial positive strokes followed by several negative strokes, and the leader electric field changes of the first positive stroke were similar to those of close negative first strokes and the return stroke electric field waveforms were similar to those observed for negative first strokes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the physical mechanisms responsible for lightning and lightning‐induced effects, with emphasis on the measurement and analysis of lightning electric and magnetic fields.
the measurement of electric and magnetic fields associated with cloud-to-ground lightning flashes.

the study of the physical properties of lightning discharges, including their initiation, propagation, and the production of lightning-generated electromagnetic fields, and their effects on the atmosphere and on man-made systems.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the bipolar lightning flash was a close negative flash that was followed by a second close negative flash, with the second negative leader traversing the same path as that for the first negative flash, but the first and second negative flashes were not connected by a common channel. [2]

the positive strokes in this flash were “close” and “negative-like” and the negative strokes were “far” and “positive-like,” but with the important difference that the negative strokes were not followed by return strokes.
this bipolar lightning flash was unusual in several ways, but not so unusual that we would not expect it to occur again in nature.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
bipolar cloud-to-ground flashes containing two positive strokes, followed by negative strokes, can be quite similar to negative first stroke flashes.
bipolar lightning flashes are not uncommon, but the bipolar flash we present is unique in that it contains a second positive stroke that is separated from the first positive stroke by about 53 ms.

bipolar cloud-to-ground flashes are not rare, that the positive first stroke is the most important for the lightning flash, that the positive leader electric field is similar to the close negative leader electric field for the first stroke, and that the positive second stroke leader electric field is smaller than that of the first stroke.
The main takeaway from our work is that
positive first strokes can have similar electric field waveforms to close negative first strokes and that bipolar flashes are not necessarily rare. [2]
the electric field changes measured for this flash are similar to those measured for close negative first and close negative second flashes, but the current waveforms are very different.
the bipolar lightning flash was not a single event, but rather a series of individual lightning flashes, each of which was associated with a leader electric field change and return stroke.
